summary.business: The Company is engaged in the cultivation and manufacture of tea, operating multiple tea estates spread across West Bengal and Assam (plus Darjeeling gardens), and sells bulk tea in both domestic and international markets. It also produces Instant Tea at a plant in Dooars, West Bengal, primarily for the international market, and has a strong presence in the domestic Packet Tea market through its own brands. It is managed and reported as a single tea business segment, and is diversifying into alternate crops, dairy and hospitality on some estates.

currentContext.expansion: No new manufacturing plant expansion is disclosed; capex-related activity centres on renewable-energy and agronomy initiatives at existing tea estates. Following completion of a Solar Power project at Nonaipara, similar solar power initiatives have been started at seven gardens in Assam (the report states a commissioning year but the specific numeral was not recoverable from the source text). The Company continued carbon-reduction and climatic-resilience initiatives — afforestation, creation of water bodies, use of bio-organic manure — and is transitioning towards renewable fuels (gas firing) and hydro power generation. The Company also continued diversification into alternate crops (ginger, garlic, turmeric) and dairy farming, launching its first branded dairy product (A2 Ghee) during the year, initially sold through online channels.

risks.note: Business is agricultural in nature and exposed to adverse and erratic weather (dry spells followed by over-wet conditions during peak growing months); total tea production declined ~15% YoY in FY26, with Dooars and Darjeeling gardens both posting double-digit production declines attributed to adverse weather.

Erratic weather led to an upsurge in pest activity even in non-traditional Assam belts, causing loss of high-value crop and higher crop-protection costs; management flags this as a continuing challenge for the industry.

risks.risk: Structural over-dependence on the domestic market / weak pricing power
risks.note: India's large domestic tea market provides a stable demand base but has also bred industry complacency, limiting the ability to consistently secure remunerative prices; tea producers (including the Company) continue to operate at the lower end of the value chain.

risks.risk: Competitive pressure from the Small Tea Grower (STG) sector
risks.note: Continued expansion of the lower-cost-structure STG sector has intensified competition and placed additional pressure on market realisations even as STGs contribute significantly to national tea production.

risks.risk: Rising input and labour cost inflation
risks.note: Rising labour/wage costs, increasing social welfare obligations, and escalating input costs (fertilizers, chemicals, fuel) continue to pose significant challenges to industry and Company cost structures, alongside subdued price realisations.

The Company undertakes transactions denominated in foreign currency (a significant portion in US Dollar and Euro), exposing it to exchange-rate fluctuation risk on recognised assets/liabilities not in its functional currency (INR).

The Company's agricultural, seasonal business exposes it to potential difficulty in meeting obligations; liquidity risk is managed through timely receivables collection, close credit-cycle monitoring and optimal inventory movement.

certifications.body:

- Trustea certified (all Dooars gardens plus Orangajuli and Nonaipara gardens in Assam)

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Tea markets, barring the final quarter of the year, remained largely unsupportive during FY26
- The plantation business — a substantial portion of Group operations — underperformed due to adverse weather conditions, unprecedented pest and disease attacks and consequent crop losses, which placed considerable pressure on overall revenues and profitability and sharply raised the cost of production
- The Instant Tea Division continued to deliver a strong performance during the year
- The Branded Tea business, following a period of restructuring, stringent cost management and profitability initiatives, recorded improved financial results despite lower sales volumes
- The Export Division made a meaningful contribution to the Group's earnings
- Collectively, the Instant Tea, Branded Tea and Export businesses generated much-needed profits and provided resilience to overall performance, enabling the Company to report a modest profit for the year despite challenges faced by the plantation segment

capital_allocation.title: Strategy & capital allocation
capital_allocation.body:
- Reviewing the long-term viability of estates/assets, including potential divestment of gardens where a sustainable return to profitability is considered highly unlikely, and disposal of some non-income-generating assets
- Actively pursuing diversification into dairy, piggery, alternate crops, solar and selective hospitality initiatives at some of the Company's estates/gardens, increasingly led by dedicated professionals rather than garden management teams
- Continued focus on cost discipline and efficiency, including increasing use of mechanisation where employee-availability constraints exist
- Medium-term strategy formulated to address current challenges and position the Group for sustainable growth and long-term value creation, with key elements: rationalisation/divestment of loss-making tea estates, strengthening productivity across existing gardens, enhancing price realisation through improved marketing and sales initiatives, expanding export opportunities, increasing investment in the branded tea business, and further strengthening Instant Tea operations
- Continued strengthening of the corporate governance framework through enhancements to policies, internal processes and oversight mechanisms
- The Board recommended, via an Ordinary Resolution proposed at the AGM, a final dividend of Rs 2 (Rupees Two) per equity share of face value Rs 10 (Rupees Ten) each for the financial year ended 31st March, subject to shareholder approval.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: No new manufacturing plant expansion is disclosed; capex-related activity centres on renewable-energy and agronomy initiatives at existing tea estates. Following completion of a Solar Power project at Nonaipara, similar solar power initiatives have been started at seven gardens in Assam (the report states a commissioning year but the specific numeral was not recoverable from the source text). The Company continued carbon-reduction and climatic-resilience initiatives — afforestation, creation of water bodies, use of bio-organic manure — and is transitioning towards renewable fuels (gas firing) and hydro power generation. A long-term agronomy programme, 'Operation Quintal', was launched to raise per-hectare yields in all future young tea plantations, with benefits expected to accrue over the medium to long term. The Instant Tea Plant at Aibheel (Dooars, West Bengal) continues to operate and contribute favourably to performance. The Branded Tea Division underwent a restructuring — relocating its office from Gurgaon to Kolkata, rationalising unprofitable brands/SKUs, and implementing more efficient tea-procurement strategies — alongside new investment in brand-building/advertising for its flagship Darjeeling and CTC brands. The Company also continued diversification into alternate crops (ginger, garlic, turmeric) and dairy farming, launching its first branded dairy product (A2 Ghee) during the year, initially sold through online channels.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Established branded packet-tea portfolio (flagship Darjeeling and CTC brands) with a strong presence in the domestic market
- Diversified business model — Instant Tea and Export divisions delivered profits and provided resilience even as the core plantation segment underperformed
- Existing pan-India distribution network being leveraged to market new diversification products (dairy, alternate crops)
- Sustainability/quality certifications (Rainforest Alliance, FSSC, Trustea) across estates supporting export and premium positioning

risks.title: Bear — key risks
risks.body:
- Weather/climate dependency of tea production — Business is agricultural in nature and exposed to adverse and erratic weather (dry spells followed by over-wet conditions during peak growing months); total tea production declined ~15% YoY in FY26, with Dooars and Darjeeling gardens both posting double-digit production declines attributed to adverse weather.
- Pest and disease incidence — Erratic weather led to an upsurge in pest activity even in non-traditional Assam belts, causing loss of high-value crop and higher crop-protection costs; management flags this as a continuing challenge for the industry.
- Structural over-dependence on the domestic market / weak pricing power — India's large domestic tea market provides a stable demand base but has also bred industry complacency, limiting the ability to consistently secure remunerative prices; tea producers (including the Company) continue to operate at the lower end of the value chain.
- Competitive pressure from the Small Tea Grower (STG) sector — Continued expansion of the lower-cost-structure STG sector has intensified competition and placed additional pressure on market realisations even as STGs contribute significantly to national tea production.
- Rising input and labour cost inflation — Rising labour/wage costs, increasing social welfare obligations, and escalating input costs (fertilizers, chemicals, fuel) continue to pose significant challenges to industry and Company cost structures, alongside subdued price realisations.
- Foreign-currency exposure on export transactions — The Company undertakes transactions denominated in foreign currency (a significant portion in US Dollar and Euro), exposing it to exchange-rate fluctuation risk on recognised assets/liabilities not in its functional currency (INR).
- Liquidity risk / business seasonality — The Company's agricultural, seasonal business exposes it to potential difficulty in meeting obligations; liquidity risk is managed through timely receivables collection, close credit-cycle monitoring and optimal inventory movement.
